raw_response:
I've been farming this land in Quzhou for 25 years. I know what works here. The soil is decent loam, winters are cold and dry, summers are hot. My well gives me water but I don't waste it — electricity for pumping costs money and water is getting harder to come by every year.

My main system is wheat-maize on 120 mu of flat land. That's what pays the bills and feeds us. I rotate them because it's what everyone around here does and the yields are reliable. The other 80 mu I split between millet and a small cabbage plot.

**Wheat (winter):** I'll sow in early October after the summer maize comes off. I've been using the same improved variety from the county seed station for years — it yields well and handles the dry springs we get. I'll plough before sowing, that's how I've always done it to break up compaction. Three irrigations: pre-sowing to settle the soil, jointing stage, and heading. Wheat here gets wheat aphids and powdery mildew, so I'll do a seed treatment plus spray twice.

**Maize (summer):** Goes in right after wheat harvest in June. I buy hybrid seed — been doing that for over a decade, the yield difference is real. I do rotary tillage, not full plough, because the ground is already loose and we're racing to get maize in fast. I'll water at emergence, tasseling, and if August is dry, once more at grain fill.

**Millet:** 60 mu on slightly sandier ground that doesn't suit wheat as well. Millet is forgiving. My grandfather grew it, I grew up with it. It needs less water than maize and I can sell it locally at a decent price. Just two irrigations if it gets dry. Traditional local variety — I save some seed each year.

**Cabbage:** 20 mu for autumn cabbage. Vegetable money comes in faster. Cabbage is labor-heavy but there are only two of us so I keep the plot manageable. Needs more water and more pesticide spraying — caterpillars and aphids hit it hard every year. I'll use an improved hybrid variety for better head weight.
